issue_from_ticket.subject: Need to rotate an exposed key
issue_from_ticket.body: One of our production keys started returning 401 at around yesterday morning without any change on our side. Other keys against the same account are still working.

items.title: API key rotation and scope management
items.passage: # API key rotation and scope management **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - A previously working key returns 401 Unauthorized - A key works for some endpoints and not others - A key needs replacing after accidental exposure ## Common causes - The key was revoked or reached its configured expiry - The key was issued with a scope that excludes the endpoint being called - The key belongs to a deleted user and was removed with the account ## Resolution

items.title: API key rotation and scope management
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Check the API keys page for the key's status and expiry. Revoked and expired keys are listed with the date and the user who acted. 2. Review the scopes attached to the key. Read-only keys cannot write, and project-scoped keys cannot reach organisation endpoints. 3. To rotate without downtime, create the replacement key first, deploy it, confirm traffic has moved, then revoke the old key. 4. If a key has been exposed publicly, revoke it immediately rather than waiting for the rotation window. ## Notes Keys issued to individual users are removed when that user is deleted. Use service accounts for anything running in production.

items.title: Handling exposed secrets and credential rotation
items.passage: # Handling exposed secrets and credential rotation **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - A key has been committed to a repository - A secret appears in application logs - A third party has reported finding a credential ## Common causes - Configuration was committed rather than referenced from the environment - The application prints its configuration during startup - A key was shared in a support ticket or a chat message ## Resolution

items.title: Responding to a suspected account compromise
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Revoke all API keys for the affected account immediately. This is disruptive and it is the correct first action. 2. Force a password reset and terminate active sessions for the affected users from the team members page. 3. Review the audit log for the period in question, filtering by the affected user, and record anything unexpected before it ages out. 4. Enable multi-factor authentication for all users if it is not already mandatory for the organisation. ## Notes Audit logs are retained for ninety days on Business plans and one year on Enterprise. Export them promptly during an investigation.

items.title: Connecting continuous integration pipelines
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Create a service account for the pipeline rather than using a personal key, so that access survives staff changes. 2. Grant the service account only the projects and permissions the pipeline needs, and review that grant when the pipeline changes. 3. Store the credential as an encrypted secret in your pipeline provider, never in the repository. 4. Test the pipeline credential separately from the deployment logic, so that authentication failures are distinguishable from deployment failures. ## Notes Service account keys do not expire by default. Set an expiry and rotate on a schedule.

result.answer:
Hi there,

I'm sorry to hear you're having trouble signing in. Since you are receiving an 'invalid credentials' message, this can sometimes be caused by the account being locked after five consecutive failed attempts, or by a stale session cookie being sent alongside your new credentials [DOC-AUTH-001]. 

Additionally, if you are using multi-factor authentication, please ensure that automatic time synchronization is enabled on the device generating your code, as clock drift of more than thirty seconds is the most common cause of rejected codes [DOC-AUTH-002]. 

Please try clearing your browser cache and cookies, or attempting to sign in from a different browser or device to rule out stale session issues [DOC-AUTH-001]. If the issue persists, please let us know if you are using MFA and if you have access to any recovery codes.

Best regards,
Support Team

issue_from_ticket.subject: Suspicious activity in audit log
issue_from_ticket.body: We have found activity in our audit log from an address none of us recognise, going back to yesterday morning. Resources were created that nobody on the team claims. We need help urgently.

items.title: Responding to a suspected account compromise
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Revoke all API keys for the affected account immediately. This is disruptive and it is the correct first action. 2. Force a password reset and terminate active sessions for the affected users from the team members page. 3. Review the audit log for the period in question, filtering by the affected user, and record anything unexpected before it ages out. 4. Enable multi-factor authentication for all users if it is not already mandatory for the organisation. ## Notes Audit logs are retained for ninety days on Business plans and one year on Enterprise. Export them promptly during an investigation.

items.title: Responding to a suspected account compromise
items.passage: # Responding to a suspected account compromise **Applies to:** All plans ## Symptoms - Unrecognised activity appears in the audit log - A user reports credentials may have been exposed - Resources were created that nobody claims ## Common causes - Credentials were reused from a service that suffered a breach - An API key was committed to a public repository - A former team member retained access after leaving ## Resolution

items.title: Audit logging and compliance evidence
items.passage: # Audit logging and compliance evidence **Applies to:** Business and Enterprise plans ## Symptoms - An auditor has requested access records - An event that should be logged cannot be found - Log retention is shorter than a policy requires ## Common causes - The event predates the retention window - The event type is not covered by the audit log - The organisation is on a plan with shorter retention ## Resolution

items.title: Audit logging and compliance evidence
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Filter the audit log by actor, resource and date range. Every administrative action carries the user, the address and the outcome. 2. Export the relevant period to object storage for anything needed beyond the retention window. Exports are not subject to retention limits. 3. Configure continuous export to your own storage if a policy requires retention longer than the plan provides. 4. Note that read access to resources is not logged on Business plans, only administrative and configuration changes. ## Notes Audit log exports are themselves audited, including the fields selected and the destination.

items.title: Handling exposed secrets and credential rotation
items.passage: ## Resolution 1. Revoke the exposed credential first. Removing it from the repository does not help, because it remains in the history. 2. Issue a replacement with the narrowest scope that still works, rather than recreating the original permissions by default. 3. Search the audit log for use of the exposed credential from unfamiliar addresses during the exposure window. 4. Add secret scanning to your pipeline so that the next occurrence is caught before it reaches a remote branch. ## Notes Never send a live credential to support. Support will never ask for one, and any credential shared in a ticket must be treated as exposed.
